title: Bonus episode: The EU enlargement game – European Council on Foreign Relations
gist: A live simulation with RE-ENGAGE researchers representing six EU candidate countries (Albania, Bosnia, Georgia, Moldova, Serbia, Ukraine) stress-tests the EU enlargement process against fictional-but-plausible shocks, surfacing structural vulnerabilities: single-member-state veto risk, competing faster offers from Turkey/China/Russia, disinformation, and post-accession democratic backsliding.

themes.theme: Structural weaknesses in the EU enlargement process

insights.claim: The simulation tests whether the EU can compete when a candidate country in economic crisis receives a faster, less conditional offer of help from Turkey, China or Russia instead of Brussels' slower, strings-attached assistance.
insights.speaker: Morten Boas, Ketevan Bolkvadze, Luka Filipović, Mathilde Giske, Jessica Hendrick, Damir Kapidzic, Roman Petrov
insights.so_what: Speed of external financial assistance, not just conditionality quality, is treated as a live competitive vulnerability for EU influence in candidate states during a crisis.
insights.locator: What happens if your economy is suddenly in crisis

insights.claim: A core scenario tested is that a candidate country can deliver every reform the EU asks for and still be blocked from the next accession step by a single member state, illustrating the unilateral veto power any one EU government holds over enlargement.
insights.speaker: Morten Boas, Ketevan Bolkvadze, Luka Filipović, Mathilde Giske, Jessica Hendrick, Damir Kapidzic, Roman Petrov
insights.so_what: The single-member-state veto is a persistent structural risk that can stall enlargement independent of a candidate country's own reform performance.
insights.locator: What if your country delivers every reform

insights.claim: The panel represents six EU candidate countries - Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Georgia, Moldova, Serbia and Ukraine - drawing on three years of RE-ENGAGE surveys, interviews and crisis simulations to inform the scenario responses.
insights.speaker: Morten Boas, Ketevan Bolkvadze, Luka Filipović, Mathilde Giske, Jessica Hendrick, Damir Kapidzic, Roman Petrov
insights.so_what: Names the specific candidate-country set the underlying RE-ENGAGE research program treats as the current EU enlargement pipeline.

insights.claim: The simulation treats disinformation exploiting public frustration with the slow pace of enlargement as a serious vulnerability, testing whether the message 'Europe never wanted you anyway' could become a winning political narrative in candidate countries.
insights.speaker: Morten Boas, Ketevan Bolkvadze, Luka Filipović, Mathilde Giske, Jessica Hendrick, Damir Kapidzic, Roman Petrov
insights.so_what: Flags anti-EU narrative contagion as a specific, testable political risk in candidate states, not just an abstract concern.
insights.quote: Can 'Europe never wanted you anyway' become a winning political message?
insights.locator: When a crisis hits, does speed matter more than values?

insights.claim: A key question raised is what stops a country's democracy from sliding backward once it has finally joined the EU and the 'prize' of membership is secured, referencing Ukraine's call for Hungarian-style 'Varangians' when backsliding strikes.
insights.speaker: Morten Boas, Ketevan Bolkvadze, Luka Filipović, Mathilde Giske, Jessica Hendrick, Damir Kapidzic, Roman Petrov
insights.so_what: Post-accession democratic backsliding (the 'Hungary problem') is treated as a live design flaw in the enlargement process rather than a one-off historical anomaly.
insights.locator: Ukraine calls for Hungarian "Varangians" when backsliding strikes

source_meta.author: Morten Boas, Ketevan Bolkvadze, Luka Filipović, Mathilde Giske, Jessica Hendrick, Damir Kapidzic, Roman Petrov
